prompt_text:
The figure summarizes how human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) evades immunity and how it can reactivate in the body. The upper schematic shows an infected cell manipulating innate and adaptive immune pathways. Viral proteins appear to block DNA sensing and interferon signaling, interfere with nuclear antiviral factors, and alter chemokine production. Other viral factors suppress antigen presentation through both MHC class I and class II, reducing activation of CD8 cytotoxic and CD4 helper T cells. HCMV also encodes chemokines or chemokine-like receptors that attract neutrophils and affect natural killer cell responses, highlighting a broad strategy to dampen host detection while shaping inflammation.

The lower network diagram focuses on latency and reactivation. Latent virus is linked to bone marrow precursors and endothelial progenitors, then to myeloid and endothelial lineages. Inflammatory cytokines, allogeneic T cells, and HCMV-specific CD4 T cells are shown as triggers that can drive cellular or clinical reactivation. Monocytes differentiate into macrophages or dendritic cells, and permissive differentiated cells such as epithelial, endothelial, or smooth muscle cells support productive infection. Natural killer cells, complement, memory B cells, and activated endothelial cells also appear integrated into this reactivation pathway, suggesting that HCMV persistence depends on interactions between hematopoietic differentiation, inflammation, and immune control.
